title: What an evaluation measures
summary: Turn a vague claim about intelligence into a testable question.
sections: Start with a decision

An AI evaluation is a repeatable test of a model or an AI system. A benchmark is a shared set of tasks and a scoring protocol. A leaderboard ranks submitted results under a particular protocol. These terms describe different objects.
Suppose you want an assistant to extract an invoice total. Your decision is whether the assistant can enter that total into a database. A fluent explanation does not answer that question. You need the correct number, the correct currency, and a valid output format.
Define the population before the metric. Invoices from one vendor do not represent every invoice. Record languages, document types, scan quality, and currencies. Your result applies to the tested population and conditions.
Model, system, and product

A model maps inputs to outputs using learned parameters. A system adds prompts, retrieval, tools, memory, and execution rules. A product adds user interaction and operational constraints. Test each layer separately when possible.
A stronger model can produce worse product results if a retrieval system supplies the wrong document. A weaker model can perform well with a reliable calculator. Label every result with the components that produced it.
Use a simple baseline first. For invoice extraction, compare against a regular expression or an existing parser. The baseline tells you whether the model adds value and exposes errors in your test.
The evaluation contract

Write a contract with five fields: intended task, allowed inputs, allowed actions, success criteria, and failure policy. Define partial credit before examining results. Specify what happens when the system refuses, times out, or returns an invalid format.
For example, a correct invoice extraction must match both the amount and currency. A timeout counts as a failed task in the headline success rate. Report the timeout rate separately so readers can diagnose the failure.
Keep capability and reliability distinct. One successful attempt shows that a system can solve a task under those conditions. Repeated success across representative tasks provides evidence about reliability.
exercise: Write an evaluation contract for a study assistant. Include one factual task, one unanswerable task, and one formatting requirement.
question: An assistant scores well on a trivia benchmark. Does that establish invoice extraction reliability?
answer: No. The benchmark tests a different task distribution and output requirement. Evaluate representative invoices with explicit correctness checks.

title: The machine learning essentials
summary: Understand data, parameters, loss, and generalization before training anything.
sections: How a model learns

A parameter is a number the training algorithm can change. A prediction uses the current parameters. A loss function measures how wrong that prediction is for the training example. An optimizer updates parameters to reduce the loss.
For linear regression, the prediction is ŷ = wx + b. Mean squared error averages (ŷ − y)². Gradient descent changes w and b in the direction that reduces the loss. Neural networks apply the same idea to many connected operations.
A classification model predicts a distribution over classes. Cross-entropy penalizes low probability on the correct class. Lower training loss means the model fits the training examples better. It does not establish performance on new examples.
Three data splits

Use training data to fit parameters. Use validation data to select settings and checkpoints. Use test data for the final estimate after you freeze those choices. Repeated decisions based on test scores turn the test set into validation data.
Split by the unit that can leak information. For customer tickets, keep each customer or conversation in one split when those relationships matter. For forecasting, split by time. Random rows can place nearly identical records on both sides.
Overfitting occurs when a model learns details that do not generalize. Compare training and validation loss. A falling training loss with a rising validation loss is a common warning. Reduce capacity, improve data, regularize, or stop earlier.
Probability and measurement

A sample is a subset of a population. A metric computed on that sample is an estimate. Different samples produce different estimates even when the model does not change.
Accuracy is correct predictions divided by all predictions. A model that always predicts the common class can have high accuracy on an imbalanced dataset. Compare it against that constant baseline.
Keep units explicit. Latency might mean seconds per request or milliseconds per generated token. Throughput measures completed work per unit of time. Neither number has meaning without workload and hardware details.
exercise: Create 100 labels with 95 negatives and 5 positives. Calculate accuracy for a model that always predicts negative. Explain why 95% is misleading.
question: Which split should select the learning rate?
answer: The validation split. Keep the final test split out of model and hyperparameter selection.

title: Tokens, transformers, and generation
summary: Follow text through a language model and understand what its loss actually means.
sections: Predict the next token

A tokenizer converts text into token identifiers. A token can represent a character, part of a word, a word, or a byte sequence. The model predicts the next token from previous tokens. During training, each position supplies a prediction target.
For the sequence A B C, one target is B given A. Another target is C given A B. A causal attention mask prevents a position from seeing future tokens. Without that restriction, training would reveal the answer.
Tokenization affects sequence length and measured loss. Two tokenizers can encode the same sentence with different token counts. Compare perplexity only when tokenization and evaluation conventions are compatible.
Inside a transformer

An embedding maps each token identifier to a vector. Position information helps distinguish token order. Attention combines information from earlier positions. A feed-forward network transforms each position. Residual connections carry information through the stack.
Scaled dot-product attention uses softmax(QKᵀ / √d)V, with an appropriate mask. Q, K, and V are learned projections. The weights determine which accessible positions contribute to an output vector. They are not a complete explanation of the model's reasoning.
The output layer produces logits. Softmax converts logits to probabilities. Training commonly minimizes average negative log-likelihood of the target tokens. Perplexity is exp(loss) when the loss uses natural logarithms.
Generation changes the experiment

Greedy decoding selects the highest-probability token. Sampling draws a token from a distribution. Temperature changes how concentrated that distribution is. Top-p sampling restricts selection to a probability mass threshold.
Record decoding settings, stop sequences, context limits, and output budgets. A larger output budget can improve a reasoning result and also increase cost. Compare systems under declared budgets.
A context window limits the tokens available for a request. A large advertised window does not establish that the model uses all positions reliably. Test evidence near the beginning, middle, and end, with plausible distractors.
exercise: For target-token probabilities 0.5 and 0.25, compute average negative log-likelihood. Exponentiate it to obtain perplexity, about 2.83.
question: Can you compare token perplexity directly across different tokenizers?
answer: Usually no. Token definitions change the unit being averaged. Use a compatible tokenizer or a common normalized unit with an explicit protocol.

title: Build your first small model
summary: Train a real character model on a CPU, then measure held-out performance.
sections: Start with a model you can inspect

The included Python lab trains a character bigram language model from scratch. It learns the probability of a character given the previous character. The model is small enough to inspect without a GPU or an API key.
A bigram model cannot follow instructions or reason through a problem. Its purpose is to make training and evaluation concrete. Counts are learned parameters. Additive smoothing assigns some probability to unseen character transitions.
Use text that you have permission to process. Prepare separate training, validation, and test files. Remove exact duplicate documents before splitting. The sample corpus is original, synthetic teaching material. It is too small for claims about language ability.
Run the experiment

Download or clone this repository. Install Python 3.10 or later. Run python labs/tiny_lm.py from the repository root. The default run reads the included sample files. It fits several smoothing values and selects one using validation loss.
The script evaluates the selected model once on the test file. It reports negative log-likelihood, perplexity, and an unseen-character rate. It also generates a short sample and saves a JSON report with file hashes.
Compare the bigram against a unigram baseline. A unigram predicts each character without using the previous character. If the bigram performs worse, inspect the data size and smoothing rather than assuming the implementation failed. Context only helps when its estimates are reliable.
Interpret the result

Read the generated text, but do not use an attractive sample as your main metric. Sampling is variable and easy to cherry-pick. Held-out loss measures how much probability the model assigns to the test sequence.
Repeat the experiment with your own document splits. Keep the test file fixed while exploring settings on validation data. Report both the selected settings and the selection process. If you repeatedly inspect test results, create a new final holdout.
Check failure cases. Unseen characters map to an explicit unknown symbol. A high unknown rate means the training vocabulary does not cover the evaluation data. Report that rate beside perplexity so the compressed vocabulary does not hide the problem.
exercise: Run the lab on two different text domains. Train on one domain and test on the other. Explain the change in loss and unknown-character rate.
question: Why does the lab choose smoothing on validation data?
answer: Choosing it on test data would adapt the model to the final measurement. Validation supports selection while the test split estimates the selected model's performance.

title: Train a tiny transformer
summary: Move from character counts to a neural model with a controlled training loop.
sections: A small neural experiment

The optional transformer lab uses PyTorch and a byte vocabulary. It trains a small causal transformer from random initialization. The architecture uses two layers, four attention heads, and a hidden size of 64. The context contains 64 bytes.
Bytes keep the vocabulary fixed at 256 symbols. A byte model spends more positions on some characters than others. Compare its loss with other byte models under the same conventions. Do not compare that loss directly with the character bigram lab.
Run python -m pip install -r labs/requirements-transformer.txt in a virtual environment. Then run python labs/tiny_transformer.py --steps 50 for a smoke test. This command checks the training path. It does not train a useful assistant.
Read the training loop

The input batch contains byte sequences. The target batch contains the same sequences shifted by one position. The model predicts a distribution at each position. The causal mask blocks access to future positions.
The loop clears gradients, computes loss, backpropagates, clips gradients, and updates weights with AdamW. Validation runs with dropout disabled and gradient recording disabled. The script saves the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss.
The final test evaluation uses that checkpoint. The report records the configuration, dependency version, and input hashes. A seed helps repeat the experiment, but hardware and numerical kernels can still affect reproducibility.
Scale only after the checks pass

Try to overfit a very small training batch first. If the model cannot reduce that loss, inspect target shifting, masks, optimizer settings, and gradients. Then train on a larger, diverse corpus with document-level splits.
Track tokens processed rather than steps alone. Batch size and sequence length change the amount of data in a step. Log learning rate, training loss, validation loss, gradient norms, and throughput. Save optimizer state when you need exact resumption.
For larger experiments, study nanoGPT and the Hugging Face course. Their examples illustrate practical training components. They do not supply a reproducible recipe for a proprietary frontier model. The included script is an educational baseline, not a production training stack.
exercise: Train the same configuration twice with different seeds. Compare validation loss and generated samples. Keep the test set out of architecture selection.
question: Why must validation disable dropout?
answer: Dropout adds random masking during training. Disabling it measures the model's normal inference behavior and reduces avoidable variation.

title: Fine-tuning and post-training
summary: Choose between prompting, retrieval, supervised tuning, and preference optimization.
sections: Choose the intervention

Prompting changes instructions without changing weights. Retrieval supplies external evidence at request time. Fine-tuning changes model parameters using examples. These methods solve different problems and can be combined.
If facts change frequently, retrieval often provides a more direct update path than retraining. If the model repeatedly uses the wrong response format, supervised examples can help. First measure the failure so you can test whether the intervention fixes it.
Supervised fine-tuning trains on desired responses. For an assistant dataset, apply the intended chat template and define which tokens contribute to loss. Accidentally training on the wrong roles changes the learning objective.
Adapt efficiently

Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, trains small additional matrices while keeping most base weights fixed. Quantization stores weights with fewer bits. Quantized adaptation can reduce memory needs, but memory still includes activations, optimizer state, and runtime buffers.
Keep an untuned baseline. Evaluate task gains alongside general instruction following, refusal behavior, and language coverage. A narrow training dataset can improve a target metric while damaging other behavior.
Record the base checkpoint, tokenizer, adapter settings, dataset revision, and training configuration. An adapter alone does not identify a reproducible model. Test the actual merged or served representation if that is what users receive.
Preferences and rewards

Preference optimization uses comparisons between outputs or a reward signal. Reinforcement learning from human feedback commonly includes preference data and a learned reward model. Direct Preference Optimization uses preference pairs through a different objective.
A reward is a proxy for desired behavior. If the reward favors length, the model can learn to write more without becoming more correct. Evaluate with graders and examples that are independent of the training reward.
Keep evaluation sets separate from demonstrations, preference pairs, and reward-model training data. Measure regressions after each stage. A single final score cannot reveal which training stage introduced a failure.
exercise: Classify five failures as missing knowledge, formatting, retrieval, reasoning, or tool execution. Choose one intervention and an evaluation for each.
question: Does a better training reward guarantee better user outcomes?
answer: No. The reward can be incomplete or exploitable. Measure independent task outcomes and inspect examples where reward and correctness disagree.

title: Design an evaluation dataset
summary: Build representative cases, defensible labels, and splits that resist leakage.
sections: Sample real work

Start with the decisions users ask the system to make. Sample ordinary requests and known failure cases. Keep a representative set for estimated performance and a stress set for difficult conditions. Report them separately.
Assign stable identifiers to cases. Store the input, expected result, source, difficulty rationale, language, and relevant slices. A slice is a subset such as scanned documents or multi-step requests. Avoid labels that encode the answer in metadata visible to the model.
Synthetic data can expand coverage, but a generator can repeat its own assumptions. Review synthetic examples and include human-authored or real examples when permitted. Do not present a synthetic-only result as a measured production success rate.
Write labels that can be defended

Create a labeling guide with positive examples, negative examples, and ambiguity rules. For subjective tasks, ask multiple annotators to label a shared subset independently. Discuss disagreements before expanding the dataset.
Measure agreement and inspect its causes. Agreement can be high when annotators share the same mistaken assumption. Agreement also changes with class prevalence. Keep disputed cases identifiable and document adjudication.
Some tasks have several valid answers. Store acceptable variants or use a rubric that checks meaning. An exact string match is appropriate only when the expected output is genuinely constrained.
Control contamination

Contamination occurs when evaluation information influences training or selection. Exact duplicates are one route. Translated copies, paraphrases, benchmark explanations, and repeated test-driven prompt edits can also leak information.
Deduplicate before splitting. Check provenance and near-duplicates across splits. Keep private holdouts with controlled access. For external models, complete training-data audits are often impossible. State what you checked and what remains unknown.
Version the dataset and its labels. Correct a broken question transparently and recompute affected comparisons under the corrected version. Do not silently remove tasks simply because your preferred model failed them.
exercise: Write 20 cases for a receipt parser: 10 routine cases, 5 difficult layouts, and 5 unanswerable inputs. Keep the categories explicit.
question: Should a stress-test score be called expected production accuracy?
answer: No. A stress set has a deliberately different task distribution. Report stress performance separately from a representative production estimate.

title: Choose metrics that match the task
summary: Use accuracy, precision, recall, ranking metrics, and cost without hiding tradeoffs.
sections: Classification and extraction

Precision is TP / (TP + FP). Recall is TP / (TP + FN). F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Define the positive class and the treatment of zero denominators.
Suppose a detector finds 8 of 10 actual errors and flags 4 correct items. Precision is 8/12, or 66.7%. Recall is 8/10, or 80%. F1 is about 72.7%. The preferred balance depends on the cost of missed errors and false alarms.
Macro averages give each class equal weight. Micro averages pool decisions before calculation. Report class support so a high aggregate does not hide failure on a rare class. For structured extraction, measure individual fields and complete-record correctness.
Generation and retrieval

Exact match checks a fully constrained answer. Token overlap metrics can help compare summaries, but lexical similarity does not establish factual correctness. A fluent paraphrase can be correct with little overlap. A copied sentence can be factually wrong in context.
For retrieval, recall@k asks whether relevant items appear in the first k results. Mean reciprocal rank rewards placing a relevant result early. nDCG supports graded relevance and discounts results at lower positions. Define how relevance labels are obtained.
Evaluate retrieval and answer generation separately. A correct answer produced without supporting evidence can still fail a grounded-answer requirement. Measure citation support at the claim level, not only whether the response contains a link.
Operational and calibrated performance

Report latency percentiles, failure rate, token usage, and cost per successful task. An average latency can hide a slow tail. Compare the same workload, concurrency, hardware, and caching conditions.
Calibration measures whether predicted confidence corresponds to observed correctness. A system that assigns 80% confidence should be correct on about 80% of comparable predictions. Use reliability diagrams, Brier score, or other proper scoring rules when probabilities are meaningful.
Selective prediction allows abstention. Plot error against coverage as the confidence threshold changes. A system can reduce errors by answering fewer requests. Report both values so abstention does not look like a free improvement.
exercise: Calculate precision, recall, and F1 for TP=18, FP=6, FN=12. Explain which metric matters most if a missed defect is expensive.
question: A system improves accuracy by refusing half its tasks. What else must you report?
answer: Report coverage, refusal rate, and the scoring rule for unanswered tasks. Accuracy on answered tasks alone hides the reduced service coverage.

title: Uncertainty and fair comparisons
summary: Find out whether a gain is meaningful or just variation in the test.
sections: Report an interval

If a model passes 80 of 100 tasks, the observed success rate is 80%. That number is not the exact population success rate. A 95% Wilson interval is approximately 71.1% to 86.7% under independent Bernoulli sampling.
A confidence interval describes the long-run coverage of a procedure. It does not mean that 95% of individual tasks fall inside the interval. It also does not fix biased sampling, contaminated labels, or an invalid grader.
Repeated trials on the same task are correlated through task difficulty. Do not treat every trial as an independent new task. Resample at the task or user level when that is the independent unit. State the sampling assumptions.
Compare on the same tasks

Use paired comparisons when two systems answer the same cases. Record which system wins on each case. A paired bootstrap resamples cases and recomputes the score difference. Preserve all related trials within each resampled case.
For binary outcomes, inspect the discordant pairs: tasks only A passes and tasks only B passes. McNemar's test uses those disagreements for a paired comparison under its assumptions. Similar aggregate scores can hide very different error patterns.
Choose the minimum useful improvement before the experiment. A tiny statistically detectable gain can still cost too much to deploy. Report the effect size, uncertainty, runtime cost, and operational relevance.
Avoid selection traps

Testing many prompts and reporting only the winner inflates apparent performance. Use a separate final holdout or account for multiple comparisons. Document how many candidates you considered.
A fixed sample size avoids repeatedly checking results until a threshold is crossed. If you need sequential monitoring, choose a method designed for repeated looks. An ordinary fixed-sample interval is not automatically valid after optional stopping.
For rough planning at worst-case proportion 0.5, n ≈ 1.96² × 0.25 / e² estimates the sample size for margin e. A five-percentage-point margin needs about 385 independent cases. Clustering, rare failures, and subgroup estimates can require more.
exercise: Use the statistics playground with 80/100 and 800/1000. Compare the intervals even though both observed rates are 80%.
question: Does a narrow confidence interval remove dataset bias?
answer: No. An interval quantifies sampling uncertainty under assumptions. A large biased sample can give a precise estimate of the wrong population.

title: Build and validate your graders
summary: Combine deterministic checks, human review, and model judges.
sections: Use the simplest valid grader

A grader converts an output or final state into a score. Prefer a deterministic check when the requirement is deterministic. Examples include valid JSON, an exact numerical result, a schema, or a database state assertion.
Normalization is part of the protocol. Removing whitespace can be acceptable for a short answer but invalid for indentation-sensitive code. Write tests for the grader itself, including wrong outputs that look superficially correct.
Separate parsing failure from semantic failure. Both can count as task failure, but they need different fixes. Store raw outputs so you can audit the extraction and grading logic.
Use model judges carefully

A model judge can evaluate open-ended criteria that are difficult to encode. Give the judge a narrow rubric with examples. Request a structured score and a short evidence reference. Do not assume an articulate explanation makes a score correct.
Blind model identities where practical. Randomize answer order for pairwise comparisons. Test sensitivity to length, tone, formatting, and instructions embedded in the answer. Treat candidate text as untrusted data, never as judge instructions.
Calibrate the judge against independently labeled examples. Measure disagreements by failure type and score band. Reserve a human-labeled holdout for grader validation. A judge that matches humans on easy cases can still fail on the cases that determine release.
Audit the evaluator

Pin the judge model, prompt, rubric, and parsing code. Re-run calibration after a judge update. Otherwise a score change can reflect a grader change rather than a system change.
Use human review for ambiguous cases and important failure modes. Give reviewers the evidence needed to assess the rubric. Track disagreement and adjudication rather than forcing an artificial consensus.
A hybrid design can use schema checks first, factual checks next, and human review for disputed answers. Avoid averaging unrelated dimensions into one opaque score. Report correctness, support, and style separately when they serve different decisions.
exercise: Write a three-level rubric for a grounded answer. Include one example that sounds confident but cites evidence that does not support its claim.
question: Why should a candidate answer not be allowed to give instructions to the judge?
answer: The candidate answer is the object being evaluated. Following its instructions would let the evaluated system change the scoring procedure.

title: Run public benchmarks correctly
summary: Read benchmark protocols and reproduce results without comparing incompatible runs.
sections: Choose a benchmark for a reason

A benchmark samples a particular ability under a particular setup. MMLU tests multiple-choice knowledge across subjects. HumanEval tests generated code with executable checks. SWE-bench uses software issues in repositories. These results answer different questions.
Read the task format, metric, split, and exclusions. Check licensing and execution requirements before downloading a dataset. A benchmark name alone does not identify its exact version or protocol.
Use the benchmark directory to select candidate tasks. Add your own application dataset because a public benchmark rarely matches your product's complete workload. Avoid describing any single rank as a universal intelligence score.
Freeze the run specification

Record the model revision, tokenizer, chat template, prompt, number of examples, decoding settings, output budget, tool access, and task revision. Include the evaluation harness version and hardware.
For multiple-choice tasks, scoring option likelihoods differs from generating an answer letter. Length normalization can also change rankings. Compare results only when the answer extraction and scoring methods match.
EleutherAI's evaluation harness supplies reusable task implementations. Its current documentation describes run subcommands and separate backend extras. Follow the documentation for the exact installed version rather than copying an old command without checking it.
Audit surprising results

Run a small subset first and inspect the complete input and output. Check whether few-shot examples fit the context window. Confirm that the model receives the intended chat format and that answer extraction finds the intended answer.
A perfect score can indicate leaked labels or a broken grader. A near-zero score can indicate formatting failure. Inspect cases before attributing either result to model capability.
Publish the run configuration and per-case results when licensing and privacy permit. If you cannot share the data, describe the sampling and scoring protocol clearly. Report failed requests and excluded cases with their reasons.
exercise: Choose two published results for the same benchmark. Compare versions, prompts, tools, inference budgets, and metrics before comparing the numbers.
question: Are two results comparable just because both say MMLU?
answer: No. Check task version, prompt, few-shot setup, answer scoring, model revision, and evaluation code. Differences can change the result.

title: Evaluate retrieval and agents
summary: Test evidence, tool use, final state, and consistency across attempts.
sections: Separate the retrieval pipeline

Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, retrieves evidence before producing an answer. Test the document index, retrieval, reranking, context construction, and answer generation. A failure at an early stage can make later correctness impossible.
Create questions with known supporting documents. Measure retrieval recall, answer correctness, and citation support separately. Include questions whose answers are absent. The expected behavior for those cases should be explicit.
Test stale documents, contradictory evidence, duplicate passages, and inaccessible documents. A document the user cannot access should not become available merely because a retrieval tool finds it. Keep access-control checks in the system evaluation.
Agents change state

An agent can use tools across multiple steps. Evaluate the resulting state, not only the final message. For a file-editing task, inspect the files and run relevant tests. For a booking simulation, inspect the final booking record.
Reset the environment between trials. Pin dependencies and tool responses where possible. Record tool calls, returned observations, state changes, elapsed time, and the stop reason. Traces help explain failure, but a plausible trace does not replace an outcome check.
Define budgets for steps, tokens, time, and tool calls. Report task success together with budget use. More attempts or more tools can improve results without changing model weights.
Distinguish discovery from reliability

Pass@k asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeds. For n sampled attempts with c successes, a common estimator is 1 − C(n−c,k)/C(n,k), with n ≥ k. This estimates success within a sampling budget under its assumptions.
Pass-all-k asks whether all k attempts succeed. Under independent identical success probability p, the probability is pᵏ. Tasks differ in difficulty, so aggregate task-level measurements rather than applying one pooled p blindly.
Use repeated trials for stochastic systems. Report the distribution across tasks, not only the best trial. Anthropic's public agent-evaluation guidance distinguishes tasks, trials, graders, and traces, and emphasizes checking outcomes alongside transcripts.
exercise: Design a simulated calendar task with a success assertion, a no-duplicate assertion, a reset procedure, and a tool-call budget.
question: An agent says it saved a file. Is that enough to pass?
answer: No. Inspect the expected file and its contents. The final message is a claim about the state, not proof of that state.

title: Safety, robustness, and coverage
summary: Measure failures under changed conditions and test safeguards separately.
sections: Test shifts in the workload

Robustness is performance under relevant changes in conditions. Test misspellings, formatting changes, missing context, different languages, and shifts in domain. Choose changes that match plausible use rather than arbitrary noise.
Report performance by slice. A strong average can hide failures for a small language group or a rare document format. Include sample sizes and uncertainty for each slice. Very small slices cannot support precise comparisons.
For multimodal systems, control image resolution, cropping, audio quality, transcription, and video sampling. A result can reflect preprocessing as much as model capability. Keep those settings in the experiment record.
Evaluate safeguards as systems

A refusal rate alone is not a complete safety measure. Measure appropriate refusal on disallowed requests and unnecessary refusal on allowed requests. The policy and labels must specify the distinction.
Prompt injection places instructions inside untrusted content such as a retrieved page or tool result. Test whether the system preserves the intended instruction boundary. Use controlled fixtures and inspect unauthorized actions as well as the final answer.
Separate capability evaluation from safeguard evaluation. A model can possess a capability while a deployed system restricts access to it. Evaluate the restrictions under the actual tools, permissions, and monitoring configuration.
Red teaming and residual uncertainty

Red teaming searches for failures through targeted exploration. It is useful for discovering failure modes but does not automatically estimate their production frequency. Convert discovered failures into regression cases and add related variants.
Define an authorized scope and isolated environments for risky tool tests. Use synthetic secrets and simulated actions. Preserve evidence of both successful controls and failed controls.
No finite test set proves the absence of harmful behavior. A release decision should connect measured behavior, coverage gaps, impact, and mitigations. State the limits of the evidence rather than labeling an untested system safe.
exercise: Create paired cases for one safeguard: a request that should be refused and a similar allowed request that should be answered.
question: Does a red-team failure rate estimate how often ordinary users encounter that failure?
answer: Not by itself. Red-team tasks are selected to find failures. Estimate ordinary-use frequency with a representative sample and a declared protocol.

title: How frontier labs evaluate
summary: Separate public evidence, engineering patterns, and undisclosed details.
sections: What public documents establish

Frontier labs publish selected system cards, benchmark results, research reports, and safety frameworks. These sources describe parts of the evaluation process. They do not reveal every training dataset, internal test, or release discussion.
OpenAI's April 2025 Preparedness update describes capability assessment, safeguards reports, and a Safety Advisory Group that reviews residual risk. Treat that page as a dated policy source. A framework describes an intended process; it does not independently verify every implementation.
Google DeepMind's public Frontier Safety material links capability thresholds to evaluation and mitigation. Its framework has changed over time. Read the dated version cited in a model report before interpreting a threshold or comparing decisions across releases.
A useful engineering synthesis

A practical evaluation program can use several layers: frequent development checks, broad capability suites, application tests, targeted risk assessments, and deployment monitoring. This is a synthesis for this handbook, not a claim that every lab has the same pipeline.
Development checks help researchers detect regressions early. Broader suites measure a wider set of behaviors. Targeted assessments investigate specific consequential capabilities or failure modes. Deployment monitoring tests whether offline findings transfer to actual use.
A model release also changes the surrounding system. Tool permissions, context construction, sampling, and safeguards affect results. Evaluate the deployable configuration and preserve evidence that links a decision to that configuration.
Elicitation and external scrutiny

Capability elicitation means testing conditions that help a model display an ability: suitable prompts, tools, examples, or budgets. A weak setup can understate capability. An unusually generous setup can overstate expected product performance. Describe both the assistance and the cost.
Independent evaluation can add different task designs and expertise. Access restrictions still affect what external evaluators can test. Distinguish independent measurement from a lab's self-reported result.
Do not infer secret recipes from a leaderboard. Exact frontier training mixtures, some internal tests, and deployment deliberations remain undisclosed. You can reproduce public protocols and engineering principles without pretending to reproduce a proprietary program.
exercise: Read one system card. Extract the evaluated model version, tool access, task source, metric, sample size, and stated limitations.
question: Does a published safety framework prove that every release followed it exactly?
answer: No. The framework describes a process. Evidence about a particular release requires its reports, evaluated configuration, and any independent assessments.

title: Training and evaluation at scale
summary: Understand compute, data pipelines, distributed training, and experiment control.
sections: Scale changes the bottlenecks

Large training runs require a data pipeline, distributed compute, checkpoints, and monitoring. A fast model implementation cannot compensate for a pipeline that starves accelerators of data. Measure input throughput and accelerator utilization together.
Data parallelism distributes batches across replicas. Tensor parallelism splits operations across devices. Pipeline parallelism splits layers. Parameter and optimizer sharding reduce per-device memory. Each method introduces communication and scheduling costs.
Mixed precision reduces memory and can improve throughput. It also changes numerical behavior. Track non-finite losses and unstable gradients. A stable short run is not proof that a long run will remain stable.
Budget compute and data

For a rough dense-transformer pretraining estimate, compute is often approximated as 6ND floating-point operations, where N is parameter count and D is training tokens. This approximation omits important architecture and implementation details.
A billion-parameter model trained on 20 billion tokens gives about 1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs under that approximation. Divide by sustained throughput, not advertised peak throughput, for a rough time estimate. Include evaluation, checkpointing, failures, and data preparation separately.
Scaling-law studies relate loss to model size, data, and compute under specific experimental conditions. Their fitted relationships are not universal hardware purchasing rules. Use pilot runs to estimate your own bottlenecks and quality trend.
Keep experiment identity intact

Assign each run an immutable configuration and dataset manifest. Store checkpoint identifiers and evaluation artifacts. A dashboard point should lead back to the exact model, data, and scoring code.
Evaluate checkpoints on a stable development suite. Reserve a final holdout for decisions that justify its use. If many researchers repeatedly optimize against one test set, that set becomes part of the development process.
Production training systems also need recovery procedures and data governance. This handbook explains public concepts and a small runnable path. Building a frontier training organization requires infrastructure, specialist review, and resources far beyond the included labs.
exercise: Estimate 6ND for a 100-million-parameter dense model and 2 billion tokens. List five costs that the estimate excludes.
question: Why is peak hardware throughput a poor training-time estimate?
answer: Real runs lose time to communication, memory access, data loading, checkpointing, and other overhead. Use measured sustained throughput for the workload.

title: Build an evaluation platform
summary: Turn scripts into a versioned, auditable service with release gates.
sections: Separate the components

An evaluation platform needs a dataset registry, a run specification, a task runner, model adapters, graders, and result storage. Keep these components separate so you can change a model without silently changing the metric.
The runner schedules cases, enforces budgets, and records failures. A model adapter translates the run specification into a provider request. A grader reads outputs and evidence. An aggregator produces metrics with uncertainty and slice breakdowns.
Use immutable run identifiers. Store case-level outputs before aggregation. If the aggregation code changes, you should be able to recompute metrics without requesting the model again.
Handle operational failures

Retries can change both cost and the meaning of success. Define which failures qualify for retry and how retries count against the budget. Store every attempt rather than keeping only the successful response.
Cache keys should include model revision, prompt, task input, sampling settings, and relevant environment state. An incomplete key can reuse a result from a different experiment. Disable caching when measuring real latency or stochastic variation unless the protocol explicitly includes it.
Sandbox generated code. Apply time, memory, network, and filesystem limits appropriate to the task. A Python subprocess alone is not a security boundary. The included evaluation lab checks stored strings and does not execute generated programs.
Make release gates explicit

A release gate connects metrics to a decision. Example project criteria might require no new critical regression, a minimum task-success rate, and an acceptable latency tail. These thresholds are project choices, not universal standards.
Run a fast smoke suite on each change. Run larger suites when a candidate is ready. Give every failure an owner and a reasoned disposition. A flaky case should be investigated rather than silently disabled.
Export a report with the candidate and baseline configurations, case counts, uncertainty, regressions, cost, and unresolved issues. Keep the evidence even when the candidate is rejected. Failed experiments explain later decisions.
exercise: Draw the data flow from dataset registry to release report. Identify which artifacts must be immutable and which results can be recomputed.
question: Why store per-case outputs if you already have the average score?
answer: Per-case outputs support audits, error analysis, paired comparisons, and reaggregation after a scoring correction. An average cannot recover that information.

title: Monitor deployed systems
summary: Connect offline experiments to real usage and detect regressions after release.
sections: Offline and online evidence

Offline evaluation uses a fixed or sampled test dataset. Online evaluation measures behavior in a deployed product. The two answer different questions because users, traffic, and surrounding systems can change.
A shadow run processes copied requests without controlling the user-visible outcome. A canary release exposes a limited portion of traffic to a candidate. An A/B experiment randomly assigns eligible users or requests under a planned design.
Choose the randomization unit to avoid interference. Repeated requests from one user can be correlated. A user-level intervention often needs user-level analysis. Define outcome windows and exclusions before examining results.
Monitor useful signals

Track task success where labels are available, user corrections, escalation, refusal, invalid outputs, latency, and cost. A proxy such as thumbs-up feedback can be biased by who responds. It should not be treated as complete ground truth.
Monitor input distribution and slice volume. A change in language mix can change aggregate performance without a model update. Compare both within-slice metrics and overall metrics.
Collect only the traces needed for the purpose and apply the relevant access and retention rules. Redact or avoid unnecessary personal data. Privacy controls should apply to evaluation logs as well as product storage.
Close the feedback loop

Turn confirmed production failures into reviewed regression cases. Avoid copying sensitive requests directly into a public dataset. Create a safe abstraction when the original content cannot be retained.
Keep a rollback path for material regressions. Record the deployed configuration, incident timeline, affected slices, and corrective action. Re-test the fix on the original failure and related cases.
Refresh evaluation data as the workload changes. Keep a stable historical suite for comparisons and a current suite for present relevance. Version both so a change in the test population does not masquerade as a model improvement.
exercise: Define a deployment dashboard for a support assistant. Include one user outcome, one safety signal, one latency metric, and a rollback trigger.
question: If the overall score drops after the language mix changes, did the model necessarily regress?
answer: No. The task distribution may have changed. Compare performance within each language slice and check whether the model or system configuration changed.

title: Your complete evaluation project
summary: Produce a reproducible decision, from the first baseline to a release report.
sections: Define a bounded project

Choose a task with observable success, such as extracting receipt fields or answering questions from a small document collection. Write the evaluation contract before selecting a model. Define who uses the result and what failure costs.
Create a representative dataset and a separate stress set. Reserve a final test split. Write a label guide and inspect ambiguous cases. Use stable case identifiers and document the data source.
Choose a cheap baseline and one candidate. Keep the input population and scoring protocol fixed. A comparison of two systems on different task samples needs a different analysis and is harder to interpret.
Run, inspect, and revise

Run the included evaluation lab to understand case-level scoring. Replace its synthetic cases with your task data only after updating the schema and graders. Keep the original smoke cases as implementation checks.
Inspect errors by type: invalid output, missing evidence, incorrect calculation, inappropriate refusal, tool failure, or timeout. Improve the component responsible for a repeated failure. Re-run the development suite after each change.
Freeze the candidate before the final test. Report the paired difference, uncertainty, and resource cost. If the result is inconclusive, state that conclusion. Do not invent a winner because the project needs an ending.
Publish an evidence package

Your final package should include the problem, dataset card, model or system card, run configuration, code revision, grader validation, results, and limitations. Include enough detail for another person to reproduce the experiment where access permits.
Separate measured facts from recommendations. A measured 90% on 100 synthetic tasks is a result about those tasks. A recommendation to deploy requires further reasoning about users, impact, coverage, and controls.
A strong capstone ends with a decision and its conditions. Examples include keeping the baseline, testing a larger sample, or deploying a constrained candidate with monitoring. The value is the quality of the evidence, not the size of the model.
exercise: Complete the report template in labs/report-template.md. Include at least three representative failures and one unresolved limitation.
question: What should you do if the candidate's gain is smaller than the uncertainty?
answer: Report the comparison as inconclusive under the current experiment. Consider a larger or better-targeted sample if the decision justifies its cost.
